title: JESUS TURNED WATER INTO WINE… SO WHY ARE SOME CHRISTIANS SAYING EVEN ONE DRINK IS A SIN?
paragraphs: JESUS TURNED WATER INTO WINE… SO WHY ARE SOME CHRISTIANS SAYING EVEN ONE DRINK IS A SIN?
The Bible's Uncomfortable Truth About Alcohol, Drunkenness, Addiction, Christian Freedom, and the Difference Between What God Permits and What Love May Ask You to Surrender.
He was sitting alone after everyone had gone to bed.
The house was quiet. His family thought he was fine. His friends knew him as a Christian. He attended church, prayed before meals, and could quote Scripture when someone needed encouragement.
But there was a bottle beside him.
And it wasn't his first.
He told himself he only needed something to help him relax. Something to quiet the pressure. Something to make the memories stop talking for a few hours.
He wasn't trying to rebel against God.
He was tired.
And somewhere between the first drink and the last, the thing he called relief had quietly become the thing he couldn't imagine living without.
The next morning, he opened his Bible.
His eyes fell on a passage about Jesus turning water into wine.
And suddenly, he had a question.
If Jesus made wine, how could drinking it be wrong?
It sounds like a reasonable question.
But there is another question hiding underneath it.
If something is permitted in Scripture, does that automatically mean it is wise for you?
Because the Bible's teaching about alcohol is far more honest, more nuanced, and more spiritually demanding than the slogans Christians sometimes throw at each other.
Some believers insist that touching alcohol is always sinful.
Others insist that because Jesus drank wine, nobody has the right to question their drinking.
But what if both arguments are missing something?
What if the real issue is not simply what is inside your glass, but what is happening inside your heart?
And what if the most dangerous thing about alcohol is not always the alcohol itself, but the moment you begin defending something that is quietly mastering you?
Stay with me.
Because before this is over, we need to walk through a wedding in Cana, a warning from Proverbs, a command from Paul, and a cross where Jesus offered a freedom far deeper than the freedom to drink.
And we need to be honest about what Scripture actually says.
Not what tradition says.
Not what culture says.
Not what our personal preferences wish it said.
What God has actually revealed.
In John 2:1–11, Jesus attends a wedding in Cana of Galilee.
The celebration is underway when something embarrassing happens.
The wine runs out.
In that culture, a wedding was not merely a private gathering. Hospitality carried enormous social significance, and running out of wine could bring shame upon the hosts.
Mary tells Jesus, "They have no wine" (John 2:3, KJV).
Jesus instructs the servants to fill six stone water jars.
And then something extraordinary happens.
The water becomes wine.
John 2:9 uses the Greek word οἶνος (oinos), the ordinary Greek word for wine.
It is important to understand this carefully.
The word oinos does not, by itself, establish the precise alcoholic strength of every beverage described by that term. Its meaning must be understood in context.
But neither does the passage provide a basis for confidently claiming that Jesus created nothing more than ordinary grape juice.
The wedding steward tastes what Jesus has provided and says:
"Thou hast kept the good wine until now." — John 2:10, KJV
The passage portrays real wine within the ordinary setting of a wedding feast.
And John identifies the miracle as the beginning of Jesus' signs, through which He manifested His glory and His disciples believed in Him (John 2:11).
That final detail matters enormously.
The purpose of the miracle was to reveal the glory of Christ, not to give Christians unlimited permission to consume alcohol.
Jesus was revealing Himself.
The miracle points toward His identity, His authority, and the joy associated with His coming.
To reduce the entire event to "Jesus made wine, so I can drink whatever I want" is to miss the greater glory standing in the room.
But to insist that every use of wine is inherently sinful also creates a serious interpretive problem.
Why?
Because Scripture itself speaks of wine in more than one way.
Psalm 104:14–15 describes God providing vegetation for human use and wine that gladdens the human heart.
In the Hebrew text, the word for wine is יַיִן (yayin).
The relevant phrase is:
וְיַיִן יְשַׂמַּח לְבַב־אֱנוֹשׁ
Ve-yayin yesammaḥ levav-enosh.
Meaning, "And wine gladdens the heart of man."
The Hebrew does not present wine here as an inherently evil substance.
It appears within a psalm celebrating God's provision in creation.
Ecclesiastes 9:7 likewise speaks of eating bread with joy and drinking wine with a merry heart, within its broader reflection on receiving life's gifts under God.
And in 1 Timothy 5:23, Paul tells Timothy:
"Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities." — KJV
The Greek expression is οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ (oinō oligō).
It means "a little wine."
Notice the restraint.
Paul does not tell Timothy to drink without limits. He gives a specific, modest instruction connected to Timothy's physical ailments.
And this passage should not be turned into a modern medical prescription for everyone. Alcohol has genuine health risks, and contemporary medical decisions require appropriate medical guidance.
Still, the biblical point remains.
If every consumption of wine were inherently sinful, Paul's instruction would be difficult to explain.
So does this mean alcohol is harmless?
Absolutely not.
And this is where some readers may become uncomfortable.
Because the same Bible that acknowledges wine as something that can be received with thanksgiving also issues terrifying warnings about what happens when human beings misuse it.
Proverbs 20:1 says:
"Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise." — KJV
The Hebrew word for wine is again yayin.
The expression for strong drink is שֵׁכָר (shekhar), referring to an intoxicating beverage.
The warning is not imaginary.
Alcohol can deceive.
It can weaken judgment, magnify foolishness, and draw people into actions they would otherwise resist.
And Proverbs 23:29–35 becomes even more graphic.
It describes sorrow, conflict, unnecessary wounds, impaired perception, and the disturbing desire to drink again after suffering alcohol's consequences.
Verse 31 warns:
"Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright."
Then verse 32 declares:
"At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder."
Read that again.
It biteth like a serpent.
The warning is not simply about a beverage.
It is about seduction.
Something can appear attractive while carrying consequences that are devastating.
Something can promise relaxation while delivering bondage.
Something can begin as a celebration and end as a prison.
And if you have ever watched alcohol destroy a marriage, fracture a family, damage a child's sense of safety, or consume a person's dignity, you know this is not merely ancient poetry.
It is painfully recognizable.
Some people know exactly what it feels like to hear a car pull into the driveway and immediately become afraid.
They know the difference between the footsteps of someone who is sober and the footsteps of someone who has been drinking.
They know what it means to love a person who becomes someone else after the bottle is opened.
They know what it feels like to receive an apology in the morning for words spoken the night before.
And they know the exhaustion of hearing, "It won't happen again."
If that describes your childhood, your marriage, or your own struggle, please understand something.
The Bible does not romanticize drunkenness.
It confronts it.
And God does not require you to pretend that alcohol-related harm is insignificant just because wine appears in certain biblical celebrations.
Ephesians 5:18 says:
"And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit." — KJV
The Greek begins:
καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ
Kai mē methyskesthe oinō.
"Do not get drunk with wine."
The verb μεθύσκεσθε (methyskesthe) concerns becoming intoxicated.
Paul is not merely offering a lifestyle suggestion.
He is giving a command.
And the contrast is profound.
Do not be controlled by drunkenness.
Be filled with the Holy Spirit.
Paul then describes a Spirit-filled life characterized by worship, thanksgiving, and mutual submission in reverence for Christ (Ephesians 5:19–21).
This is not a promise that a Christian will never experience temptation.
It is a call to live under the Spirit's influence rather than surrendering oneself to intoxication.
Galatians 5:19–23 reinforces the distinction.
Drunkenness appears among the works of the flesh, while self-control appears among the fruit of the Spirit.
The Greek word translated "drunkenness" in Galatians 5:21 is μέθαι (methai).
And the word translated "temperance" or "self-control" in Galatians 5:23 is ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia).
Self-control is not a minor Christian virtue.
It is part of the Spirit's work in a transformed life.
So here is the biblical distinction we must not erase.
Scripture does not universally condemn every instance of drinking wine. Scripture does clearly condemn drunkenness.
And beyond drunkenness, Scripture calls believers to wisdom, sobriety, self-control, love, and responsible stewardship of their bodies and relationships.
That means the question is bigger than whether one sip is automatically sinful.
It includes what you are doing, why you are doing it, what it is doing to you, and whether your actions honor Christ.
Now consider something even more uncomfortable.
A person can defend a behavior as technically permissible while ignoring the damage it causes.
Paul addresses this deeper problem in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
"All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any." — KJV
Paul is responding to claims about freedom in the Corinthian church, not issuing a blanket approval of every conceivable behavior.
But his principle is unmistakable.
Not everything claimed as permissible is beneficial.
And the believer must not willingly become mastered by anything.
The Greek phrase near the end of the verse is:
οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος
Ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos.
"I will not be mastered by anything."
That is a devastating sentence when placed beside addiction.
Because there is a difference between saying, "I am free to drink," and being genuinely free to walk away.
There is a difference between enjoying something and needing it.
There is a difference between a choice and a compulsion.
And there is a difference between Christian liberty and using Christian liberty to excuse self-destruction.
Imagine someone saying, "Alcohol doesn't control me."
But they cannot get through an evening without it.
They cannot celebrate without it.
They cannot face disappointment without it.
They cannot process grief without it.
They cannot sleep without it.
And every time a loved one expresses concern, they become defensive.
Not every person who drinks has an alcohol problem. Nor can dependence be diagnosed from one habit or one conversation.
But if your relationship with alcohol is becoming compulsive, secrecy is increasing, or your life is suffering because of it, that deserves serious attention.
And if physical dependence has developed, suddenly stopping alcohol can be medically dangerous. Seeking professional medical help is wisdom, not spiritual failure.
You can pray and receive treatment.
You can trust Christ and seek counseling.
You can confess your struggle and accept practical support.
God's grace is not threatened by the existence of doctors, recovery programs, or trustworthy people who walk beside you.
In fact, one of the bravest prayers a struggling believer can offer is painfully simple.
"Lord, I need help."
Not because those words are magical.
But because they replace denial with truth.
And the Gospel does not require us to manufacture an appearance of strength.
It calls us to come to Jesus.
Yet there is another side of this conversation that the church must confront.
We must not condemn as universally sinful what Scripture itself does not universally forbid.
Romans 14 addresses disagreements over food, days, conscience, and conduct before God.
The chapter does not primarily discuss modern drinking habits, but its principles about conscience and love are relevant.
Romans 14:21 says:
"It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak." — KJV
Notice what Paul is teaching.
There are circumstances in which voluntarily abstaining from something otherwise permissible is the loving choice.
Christian freedom is not merely the ability to insist on one's rights.
Sometimes it is the willingness to surrender a right for another person's good.
Imagine sitting across from someone who has spent years fighting alcohol dependence.
You may be capable of drinking moderately without becoming intoxicated.
But your friend is newly sober.
And drinking in front of that person may place unnecessary pressure on an already difficult struggle.
What does love do?
Does it announce, "The Bible says I'm allowed"?
Or does it quietly put the glass aside?
Not because the glass is necessarily sinful.
But because your brother or sister matters more than proving a point.
Love is not weakened when freedom is voluntarily restrained. Sometimes that is precisely how love becomes visible.
And to believers who abstain completely, hear this as well.
Your decision can be wise, holy, compassionate, and deeply honorable.
You may abstain because of personal conviction.
Because of family history.
Because of a previous addiction.
Because of a commitment to sobriety.
Because of your responsibilities.
Because of concern for others.
Or simply because you believe abstinence is the wisest way for you to glorify God.
You do not need to apologize for that decision.
But neither should personal abstinence automatically become a universal command that Scripture has not given to every believer.
The Bible contains particular abstinence requirements and vows, including the Nazirite vow in Numbers 6 and the restrictions given to priests serving in the sanctuary in Leviticus 10:9.
Those passages show that abstinence can carry serious spiritual significance in specific contexts.
They do not establish that every believer, in every circumstance, is under an identical prohibition.
And while some Christians understand their convictions or church commitments to require complete abstinence, we should distinguish those commitments from an explicit universal biblical ban.
Faithfulness requires both conviction and accuracy.
We should never weaken God's warnings.
But we should not strengthen our own preferences into commandments and then claim that God spoke words He did not speak.
That is not reverence for Scripture.
Reverence means allowing Scripture to say exactly what it says.
No less.
And no more.
Now there is a moment in the Gospels that makes this discussion even more revealing.
In Luke 7:33–34, Jesus contrasts the reactions people had toward John the Baptist and toward Himself.
John came abstaining from wine and was accused of having a demon.
Jesus came eating and drinking and was accused of being a glutton and a drunkard.
The accusations were hostile judgments made against Jesus, not reliable descriptions of His character.
But the contrast does show that Jesus' ordinary social conduct differed from John's abstinent lifestyle.
And the point of Jesus' words is striking.
Some people were determined to reject God's messengers regardless of their behavior.
If John abstained, they criticized him.
If Jesus participated in ordinary meals, they criticized Him.
The problem was not simply what was being consumed.
It was the hardness of hearts unwilling to receive God's wisdom.
And we need to be careful that our conversations about alcohol do not become another opportunity to attack people while overlooking the condition of our own souls.
A person can refuse every alcoholic drink and still be consumed by pride.
Another can defend moderate drinking while being consumed by selfishness.
One can turn abstinence into self-righteousness.
Another can turn freedom into an excuse for recklessness.
Neither attitude reflects the fullness of Christlike maturity.
The Christian life is not a competition over who can appear more righteous.
It is a life of repentance, faith, obedience, humility, and love.
And that brings us to the question beneath all the other questions.
What are you actually looking for when you reach for the glass?
For some, the answer may be ordinary enjoyment within responsible limits.
We should not invent guilt where Scripture does not establish it.
For others, the answer may be harder to admit.
"I want to stop thinking."
"I want to feel brave."
"I want to forget what happened."
"I want to stop feeling lonely."
"I want to silence the guilt."
"I want one night when my life doesn't hurt."
And this is where the conversation becomes deeply personal.
Because the Gospel speaks to wounds that no bottle can ultimately heal.
Alcohol may temporarily change how someone feels.
It cannot forgive sin.
It cannot reconcile a person to God.
It cannot restore a wounded conscience.
It cannot become the Savior of a human soul.
Only Jesus Christ can save sinners.
And He did not come merely to improve our coping mechanisms.
He came to reconcile us to God through His death and resurrection.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." — KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we had conquered every temptation.
Not after we had learned to look respectable in church.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.

And if you have fallen into drunkenness, if you have hurt people, if you have broken promises, if you have hidden bottles, or if you have repeatedly told God you would change and then stumbled again, that verse is not an excuse to continue in sin.
It is an invitation to come out of hiding.
Repentance does not mean pretending the consequences never happened.
It means turning toward God in truth, trusting Christ, and beginning to walk in the new life His grace makes possible.
Sometimes that includes apologizing.
Sometimes it includes making restitution.
Sometimes it includes rebuilding trust over time.
Sometimes it means avoiding alcohol entirely.
Sometimes it means admitting that recovery will require long-term treatment and support.
And sometimes it means hearing from someone you love, "I forgive you, but I still need boundaries."
Grace does not cancel wisdom.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust.
And genuine repentance does not demand that wounded people ignore their safety.
But the mercy of Christ reaches people whose stories have become painfully complicated.
Think about 1 Corinthians 6:9–11.
Paul includes drunkards among those whose sinful patterns are incompatible with inheriting God's kingdom.
That warning must be taken seriously.
But then he turns toward the Corinthian believers and says:
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God." — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
Such were some of you.
Three words that carry extraordinary hope.
The Corinthians were not a gathering of people who had never sinned.
They were people who needed cleansing.
People who needed redemption.
People whose past did not have the final word because of Jesus Christ.
And this is the heartbeat of the Gospel Warrior message.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because consequences disappeared.
Not because human beings could save themselves through willpower.
But because Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose from the dead, and offers forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in faith.
The cross is not permission to remain enslaved.
It is the proclamation that sin and shame do not have to define the rest of your story.
And the resurrection declares that death itself does not have the final word.
There is a beautiful irony here.
At Cana, Jesus turned water into wine.
At Calvary, Jesus gave His own life to redeem sinners.
And at the Last Supper, He took the cup and spoke of His blood of the covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:27–28).
The significance of that cup was not an invitation to intoxication.
It pointed toward His sacrificial death.
The deepest gift Jesus offers is not something that temporarily changes your mood.
It is reconciliation with God through His blood.
And that is why the central question cannot be reduced to, "How much alcohol can I consume before it becomes sinful?"
A more faithful question is:
"Lord Jesus, how can I honor You with my body, my decisions, my relationships, my freedom, and my entire life?"
First Corinthians 10:31 says:
"Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." — KJV
Whether you eat.
Whether you drink.
Whatever you do.
Do it for God's glory.
That command reaches both the Christian who drinks moderately and the Christian who abstains.
It challenges the person who wants to justify intoxication.
And it challenges the person who wants to boast about abstinence.
It asks whether our choices are governed by gratitude, holiness, wisdom, self-control, and love.
It asks whether we are obeying the Lord or defending ourselves.
It asks whether our actions help us serve others or make us careless toward them.
It asks whether we are living as people redeemed by Christ.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part is this:
Sometimes the most spiritual decision you can make is not to prove that you are allowed to do something.
It is to recognize that you do not need to do it.
There is no shame in saying, "For me, the wisest choice is not to drink."
There is no shame in saying, "My family has suffered enough from alcohol."
There is no shame in saying, "I cannot safely return to that habit."
There is no shame in saying, "I want to be fully present for my children."
There is no shame in saying, "I am choosing abstinence because I love God and want to protect my recovery."
And there is no biblical justification for condemning every believer merely because they have responsibly consumed wine, as though Scripture had plainly forbidden all such consumption.
We must be truthful.
Drunkenness is sin.
Addiction and harmful drinking must be taken seriously, without treating every person with a substance-use disorder as morally identical or reducing a complex medical condition to a lack of faith.
Moderation does not automatically guarantee wisdom or safety.
Abstinence can be a profoundly wise and loving choice.
Christian liberty must never become an excuse for harming ourselves or others.
And our ultimate hope must never be placed in a substance, a personal rule, or a religious reputation.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
Maybe you came into this article wanting someone to settle an argument.
Maybe you wanted proof that all alcohol is sinful.
Maybe you wanted proof that nobody should ever question your drinking.
Maybe you came because someone you love is struggling.
Or maybe you are the one struggling.
And nobody knows.
You have learned how to smile in public and unravel in private.
You know how to say, "I'm okay," while silently wondering how much longer you can keep going.
You have promised yourself that tomorrow will be different.
But tomorrow keeps looking like yesterday.
Please hear this.
You do not have to wait until your life is completely destroyed before asking for help.
You do not have to reach the bottom before turning toward Christ.
You do not have to make your suffering dramatic enough to deserve compassion.
And you do not have to face recovery alone.

If alcohol is taking more from your life than you are willing to admit, tell someone trustworthy. Speak with a qualified professional. Seek the support of a healthy Christian community that understands both the seriousness of sin and the complexity of addiction.
And bring your struggle honestly before God.
Not with polished religious language.
With truth.
"Jesus, I need You."
"Jesus, forgive me."
"Jesus, teach me to walk in freedom."
"Jesus, help me take the next right step."
That is not a performance.
It is the beginning of honesty before the One who already knows your heart.
And if this article has exposed something you have been avoiding, I want to invite you to respond.
Not for appearances.
Not to impress anyone.
But because someone else reading the comments may need to know they are not the only person fighting a battle nobody sees.
You do not need to reveal private details, identify someone else's addiction, or confess anything publicly that would put you at risk. You can also reach out privately to someone safe.
And if God has helped you walk away from destructive drinking, consider sharing a brief testimony.
Not to glorify your past.
But to glorify the Savior who met you in it.
Someone reading may be only one honest conversation away from seeking help.
Someone may have spent years believing they are beyond redemption.
Someone may need to hear that Christ's mercy is real and that change is possible, even when recovery takes time.
Return to it when conversations about alcohol become confusing, when personal convictions are challenged, or when you need to remember the difference between Christian freedom and spiritual bondage.
Not simply because it may reach more people, but because your willingness to share biblical truth could help someone wrestle honestly with a question they have been afraid to ask.

And if one particular friend or family member comes to mind, consider tagging them with sensitivity—or send it privately if the subject is personal. Never use someone's struggle as a public spectacle.
Some people need correction.
Some need comfort.
Some need a reminder that the church is called to speak truth with love.
And some desperately need to hear that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to win arguments for the sake of winning.
Not to make people feel religious for a few minutes.
But to keep pointing wounded, searching, struggling, and growing people back to Jesus Christ and the authority of His Word.
And if you want to help this ministry continue and expand, I want to invite you into something deeper.
It is not a requirement for being a faithful Christian.
It is not a substitute for repentance, obedience, or participation in the life of a local church.
And it is not a biblical obligation that every believer must fulfill.
But it can be a meaningful, voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel-centered ministry.
Scripture teaches that believers may generously support those who labor in teaching and proclaiming the Gospel (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
It should not be presented as a replacement for any tithing or giving commitment you believe you have toward your local church. Your responsibilities to your family and essential needs also matter.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
The free resources are there to help you grow.
Because the goal is not to build a community that merely agrees with every post.
The goal is to encourage people to know Scripture, follow Jesus, grow in holiness, and carry the truth of the Gospel into their everyday lives.
And before you leave, I want you to remember the man sitting alone beside the bottle.
Maybe he represents someone you know.
Maybe he represents someone you used to be.
Maybe, painfully, he represents you.
He began with a question about whether drinking was allowed.
But perhaps the question he most needed to ask was whether he was truly free.
And perhaps that is the question some of us need to carry before God tonight.
Not, "How close can I get to sin without crossing the line?"
But, "Jesus, what would it look like to surrender this part of my life to You?"
Because you can spend years defending your right to hold something that is quietly destroying you.
And you can spend years judging what is in someone else's glass while refusing to confront the pride in your own heart.
Christ calls us beyond both.
Beyond careless indulgence.
Beyond self-righteous condemnation.
Beyond religious appearances.
Into truth.
Into repentance.
Into love.
Into freedom shaped by the Holy Spirit.
Into a life where the glory of God matters more than winning the argument.
So, is drinking alcohol always sinful?

No. Scripture does not teach that every instance of consuming alcohol is inherently sinful. But it does condemn drunkenness, warn repeatedly about alcohol's dangers, and call every believer to wisdom, self-control, love, and a life that glorifies God.
And for some people, especially those vulnerable to addiction or serious harm, complete abstinence is not merely a reasonable option.
It may be the wisest and safest path.
But whatever your personal circumstances, never forget this.
Jesus did not come merely to settle the debate over what you can put in your glass.
He came to save sinners and make them new.
And if the thing you keep reaching for is slowly taking your life away, remember that the Savior who calls you into the light is not asking you to face the darkness alone.
The most dangerous prison is the one you keep calling freedom—and the most beautiful beginning is the moment you finally bring its keys to Jesus.
